text: Track 4.1 Hello everyone, my name is Wacabi Labou. I live in the United Kingdom and my family comes from Kenya, which is a large country in East Africa. My talk today is about an environmental problem in Kenya. First, I'm going to explain the issue and then I'd like to tell you about an organization which has found a successful way of dealing with the situation. So, back in the 1970s, women living in rural areas of Kenya, that is, living in the countryside, became very worried. You see, they had always collected fresh water from local streams, but now these streams were mostly dry. For this reason, the women had to walk a much greater distance every day just to fetch the water their families needed, and also to find wood for their fires. Their access to food had become more difficult too. Why was all this happening? The explanation was deforestation. What do we know about deforestation? Well, we now have a lot of data about the negative impact of deforestation on the environment. The fact is that our planet cannot survive without trees. When trees are cut down, it harms the ecosystem. It damages the soil, which means that crops cannot grow properly. It can affect the availability as well as the quality of fresh water. It affects climate change, and the result is that less rainfall. Of course, deforestation also causes local wildlife to decline because of habitat destruction. Fortunately, a solution was found thanks to an extraordinary Kenyan woman called Wangari Maffai. She was a professor and a politician who really cared about the environment and conservation. She understood the impact of destroying the forests in Kenya. She knew it meant that crops would stop growing, rivers would stop flowing, and that wildlife in these areas would disappear. Due to loss of habitat. So, in 1977, Wangari Maffai set up an environmental organisation called the Green Belt Movement. Belt is just another word for area, by the way. The Green Belt Movement, or GBM, had a plan that was quite simple. Local women were encouraged to start planting trees. Science shows that if people plant more trees, the ecosystem will begin to repair itself. And, since 1977, GBM communities have planted over 51 million trees in Kenya. I think it's incredible that these communities came together to achieve their goal. The work was mainly done by women, and, as the trees grew, the Green Belt Movement also grew. This growth then made it possible for the organisation to run environmental classes for the public. Through the GBM, Professor Maffai organised classes and seminars to teach people about the connection between human activity and the environment. She knew that if the public learned about this link and the effect it has on their lives, it would make them want to change their behaviour and solve their environmental problems. Over the years, the Green Belt Movement has developed a climate change programme, with the aim of giving people in rural communities a greater understanding of the issues, and even better, helping them to see that they have the ability and the power to work against climate change. When Garimaffai was an amazing person, she achieved many important things in her lifetime, and her environmental work has made an enormous difference to the people of Kenya. It is not surprising, therefore, that she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004, and she was the first African woman to receive this great award, you know. She died in 2011, but the Green Belt Movement continues to protect and improve the environment in Kenya. And the message I want to leave you with today is that everyone, all of us, can do something to help stop environmental damage where we live, and around the world. Thank you for listening.
